6.text: The shaman Scratching-Woman also pretended to treat his patients all

7.text: the time in this way. For this purpose he used a special knife, represented

8.text: in Fig. 290. This is an ordinary iron knife set into an uncouth block of

9.text: wood with two circular notches and a double tassel of curried leather. A bead

10.text: of blue glass almost as large as a hen’s egg is also tied to the handle. The

11.text: bead looks quite old, and Scratching-Woman asserted that it was received by

12.text: his grandfather directly from the keˊlet. The handle of the knife has some

13.text: rusty spots, which were said by the shaman to be produced by the blood of

14.text: patients operated upon with the knife. Together with the knife a small flat

15.text: piece of ivory (Fig. 291) was used, which was said to be employed, as a

16.text: rule, in cutting open the body. The shaman said

17.text: it was a present from the Milky may.¹ Three

18.text: leather images were fastened to the ivory. One

19.text: was said to represent a keˊlᴇ from the “direction”

20.text: of the darkness, with the arms longer than the

21.text: legs. The middle image — with only one arm

22.text: and one leg, and the eyes standing one over the

23.text: other — represented the keˊlᴇ Iuˊmetun.² The

24.text: third image represented a crawling “spell,” which

25.text: one of the enemies of the shaman sent to attack

26.text: him; but he intercepted it on the way and

27.text: thoroughly subdued it, so that it began to do his

28.text: bidding. With the aid of these instruments,

29.text: Scratching-Woman pretended to have cut open

30.text: and put to rights internal organs, backs, shoulder-

31.text: blades, and several other parts of the bodies of many

32.text: patients, although, according to his neighbors, he

33.text: was too young to claim so many successful cases of treatment.
